source: He, Kirschbaum, Kasiviswanathan (2026) Global Consistency Repair for Natural-Language Claim Sets (QXR)
finding: QXR uses an LLM as a noisy consistency oracle, finds minimal conflicting claim subsets with QuickXplain, then deletes a small greedy hitting set. This is the Reiter conflict-then-hitting-set loop run on natural-language claims.
numbers: Claim sets of about 30 claims. Single oracle call per query (r=1), temperature 0.0, Amazon Bedrock, scope C={F}.
limits: Theory assumes a monotone, perfect judge. Experiments use one LLM call and no voting.
agent_relevance: Direct template for an agent step: find a conflict set, then repair by hitting set.

source: He, Kirschbaum, Kasiviswanathan (2026) Global Consistency Repair for Natural-Language Claim Sets (QXR)
finding: Direct all-at-once LLM judging over-prunes. It detects that something is inconsistent but removes too many claims, so recall of valid claims is low while precision stays high.
numbers: VitaminC (24-32 claims, 2-6 injected contradictions): Sonnet 4.5 direct recall 0.617 vs QXR 0.957; Opus 4.6 direct recall 0.574 vs QXR 0.968; Mistral Large 2 0.603 vs 0.978; Sonnet 3.7 0.854 vs 0.975.
limits: Gold MUSes are injected size-2 pairs; easy structure.
agent_relevance: Ask the model to localize the conflict first, never to 'return the coherent subset' in one shot.

source: He, Kirschbaum, Kasiviswanathan (2026) Global Consistency Repair for Natural-Language Claim Sets (QXR)
finding: F1 gain from QXR is large on VitaminC and small on FEVER, where direct judging is already strong. Opus 4.6 direct F1 on VitaminC was 0.611, QXR 0.976.
numbers: VitaminC F1 direct->QXR: Sonnet 3.7 .912->.965; Sonnet 4 .915->.960; Sonnet 4.5 .762->.966; Opus 4.6 .611->.976; DeepSeek-R1 .837->.981; GPT-OSS-120B .954->.975; Mistral Large 2 .739->.972. FEVER: Opus 4.6 .989->.964 (QXR slightly worse); Sonnet 4.5 .944->.962.
limits: On FEVER the structured method can lose to direct judging for the strongest models. Authors say QXR is a preservation-oriented option when extra oracle calls are justified.
agent_relevance: Use the structured loop where the set is mostly coherent with a few sparse conflicts; skip it when direct judging is already reliable.

source: He, Kirschbaum, Kasiviswanathan (2026) Global Consistency Repair for Natural-Language Claim Sets (QXR)
finding: Stronger prompting does not fix over-pruning. Chain-of-thought, decomposition, few-shot and self-consistency on the direct baseline all keep high precision and low recall.
numbers: VitaminC subset, recall: zero-shot Sonnet 3.7 .681, CoT .684, decomposition .626, few-shot .658, self-consistency .547. GPT-OSS-120B recall: zero-shot .876, self-consistency .475. Mistral Large 2 few-shot F1 .178. QXR recall .975/.995/.978 for Sonnet 3.7/GPT-OSS/Mistral.
limits: Run on a subset of the data; baseline numbers restated from the full run.
agent_relevance: Self-consistency voting made recall worse here. The fix is structure (conflict localization), not more samples.

source: He, Kirschbaum, Kasiviswanathan (2026) Global Consistency Repair for Natural-Language Claim Sets (QXR)
finding: On RAMDocs (RAG with conflicting retrieved evidence, N=30, 10 gold conflicts) QXR raised recall and F1 for small and mid-size models.
limits: Sonnet 4.5 did not gain on RAMDocs (F1 .882 vs .870). Precision dropped for Sonnet 4.5 (.962->.887).
agent_relevance: Structured conflict localization may compensate for weak set-level reasoning in smaller models.

source: He, Kirschbaum, Kasiviswanathan (2026) Global Consistency Repair for Natural-Language Claim Sets (QXR)
finding: Query complexity of the loop: with QuickXplain each MUS costs O(k log N) oracle calls, total O(I*m*(1+k log N)). Pairwise checking needs N(N-1)/2 calls.
numbers: Pairwise: 435 calls at N=30, 4,950 at N=100. Greedy hitting set has the standard log-factor approximation (Lemma A.1).
limits: Worst case still has exponentially many MUSes; minimum-deletion repair is NP-hard as hitting set. Authors note exact repair gets expensive for large claim sets.
agent_relevance: Budget for an efficient diagnosis step: log-many subset queries per conflict, not quadratic pairs.

source: He, Kirschbaum, Kasiviswanathan (2026) Global Consistency Repair for Natural-Language Claim Sets (QXR)
finding: Authors state the LLM oracle may be noisy, prompt-sensitive or non-monotonic, which breaks QuickXplain's guarantees. They sketch a graded oracle and weighted hitting set as future work.
numbers: Weighted version replaces min-cardinality hitting set with min-weight hitting set (weights w(f)>=0).
limits: Not tested empirically. No majority voting used in experiments.
agent_relevance: Weighted hitting set is a natural place to put source reliability or confidence.

source: Rodler (2020/2022) Sound, Complete, Linear-Space, Best-First Diagnosis Search (RBF-HS)
finding: RBF-HS adapts Korf's recursive best-first search to Reiter's hitting-set tree. It is sound, complete, best-first and uses linear memory, so it can return the ld best minimal diagnoses without storing the whole tree.
numbers: Compared with HS-Tree on 12 real knowledge-base debugging problems (Koala 42 axioms up to Cton 33,203 axioms); ld in {2,6,10,20}; 5 sequential diagnosis sessions per setting; Pellet reasoner; min-cardinality diagnoses; 1200 s limit.
limits: Tested on min-cardinality search; most-probable-first search trades memory savings roughly one to one for runtime overhead (per IJCAI 2023 summary).
agent_relevance: Linear-memory best-first search is the reference design for any agent that must enumerate ranked hypotheses under a context budget.

source: Rodler (2020/2022) Sound, Complete, Linear-Space, Best-First Diagnosis Search (RBF-HS)
finding: Memory savings are large, runtime cost is often small, and sometimes RBF-HS is faster.
numbers: Space saved up to 98%; runtime savings up to more than 88% (case D,20); in 4 of 10 cases RBF-HS was faster than HS-Tree; some runtime overheads reached 4900% in the worst cases.
limits: Gains grow with problem size; trivial cases show little benefit. Run on knowledge-base debugging only, not circuits.
agent_relevance: Memory is the binding constraint more often than time; same logic applies to prompt context.

source: Rodler (2020/2022) Sound, Complete, Linear-Space, Best-First Diagnosis Search (RBF-HS)
finding: Dataset spans very different diagnostic structure: from 6 to 1,566+ minimal diagnoses, min size 1-9, and logics from ALCN to SROIQ (2-NEXPTIME-complete consistency check).
numbers: Table 2: Koala 10 diagnoses; University 90; IT 1045; UNI 1296; Economy 1782; DBpedia 864; Cton 1566+ (found within 1200 s by HS-Tree).
limits: Same DPI used with no background knowledge or measurements at start.
agent_relevance: Number of candidate explanations can be huge, so only the best ld should be held.

source: Rodler (2023) Memory-Limited Model-Based Diagnosis (Extended Abstract), IJCAI 2023 journal track
finding: IJCAI 2023 journal-track abstract of the RBF-HS paper (AIJ). Seen only as a search snippet this session, not read in full. Adds a hybrid HBF-HS to cut runtime overhead.
numbers: Pages 6954-6958. Snippet: memory down by up to several orders of magnitude for min-cardinality; for most-probable-first, memory saving is about matched by runtime overhead.
limits: Snippet only; the task brief attributes the work to Jannach et al. but the abstract is by Rodler alone.
agent_relevance: Background; the brief's attribution should be checked.

source: Rodler (2020) DynamicHS: Streamlining Reiter's Hitting-Set Tree for Sequential Diagnosis
finding: DynamicHS keeps and updates the hitting-set tree across sequential diagnosis steps instead of rebuilding it. It answers a 1987 question by Reiter about reusing the tree after new measurements.
numbers: DynamicHS faster than HS-Tree in 96% of sessions and 99.4% of scenarios; median time saving 52%, maximal 75%; in the hardest cases median 64%, max 89% savings.
limits: Savings do not depend on number of diagnoses or the measurement heuristic. Knowledge-base debugging data only.
agent_relevance: Reuse state across turns instead of re-deriving candidates: supports a persistent hypothesis store in the agent loop.

source: Rodler (2020) DynamicHS: Streamlining Reiter's Hitting-Set Tree for Sequential Diagnosis
finding: Reasoner calls are the real cost. DynamicHS cuts hard and medium reasoner operations, replacing them with easy ones, and keeps all HS-Tree properties.
numbers: Reduction of hard operations 57% and medium operations 44% for some easy ones; easy calls finished faster than medium ones in 77% of cases; hardest cases avoided median overhead over 175% and max over 800%.
limits: Characterization of 'hard/medium/easy' calls is ad hoc.
agent_relevance: In an LLM agent, model calls play the role of reasoner calls; minimize and cheapen them.

source: Rodler and Elichanova (2020/2022) Do We Really Sample Right in Model-Based Diagnosis?
finding: Best-first samples of diagnoses are biased estimators, yet they are standard in sequential diagnosis. The paper compares best-first, random, worst-first and approximate-random samples.
numbers: Larger sample size improves theoretical representativeness, but no general significant gain in practical performance (number of measurements); in some cases (MPS heuristic) more diagnoses meant more measurements. Exact random sampling was best for estimation in 75% of cases; best-first was best for probability estimation in 63% and second best in 25%.
limits: Brute-force random samplers; several correlations not significant at alpha=0.05.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a bigger candidate list helps; a small ranked set is often enough.

source: Rodler and Elichanova (2020/2022) Do We Really Sample Right in Model-Based Diagnosis?
finding: Time vs information trade-off: the sampler that is fastest is not the one giving the fewest measurements. QuickXplain-based approximate random sampling matched real random sampling in effect.
numbers: In all but one scenario (SPL) a different sample type minimized time than minimized number of measurements. Approximate random (ard) was overall winner for 20 or 50 diagnoses.
limits: Four heuristics tested (ENT, SPL, RIO, MPS); recommendations depend on the heuristic.
agent_relevance: Cheap approximate candidate generation can be as effective as exact.

source: Rodler (2022/2024) How should I compute my candidates? A taxonomy and classification of diagnosis computation algorithms
finding: Taxonomy of diagnosis computation algorithms by features such as completeness, soundness, best-first order, space efficiency, and reasoner independence. Notes that when memory is the scarcer resource, trading time for space (RBF-HS style) is the right choice.
numbers: Lists space efficiency as feature 12 (worst-case memory polynomial vs exponential).
limits: Taxonomy only; no new experiments. No LLM content.
agent_relevance: Gives a checklist for choosing a candidate generator for the agent's hypothesis step.

source: Rodler (2023) Don't Treat the Symptom, Find the Cause! Efficient AI Methods for (Interactive) Debugging (habilitation)
finding: Habilitation thesis that collects Rodler's work: efficient diagnosis computation, sequential diagnosis with query selection, and user-facing ontology debugging. Mentions misleading fault information as a failure case.
numbers: Thesis, Dec 2022. No mention of language models (0 hits for LLM/GPT).
limits: Skimmed, not read in full.
agent_relevance: Pre-LLM baseline; shows the field has no LLM evaluation before 2023.

source: Rodler, Jannach, Schekotihin, Fleiss (2019) Are Query-Based Ontology Debuggers Really Helping Knowledge Engineers?
finding: Human user study of query-based ontology debugging (OntoDebug, Protege). Users make oracle errors and often fail to recognize the true fault even when the debugger ranks it first.
numbers: Study 1: 29 participants (computer science students); average 28 min, 81 mouse clicks; 77% of the 5 injected faulty axioms found (SD 21%); 10 of 29 (34.4%) found the full true diagnosis.
limits: Student sample; two small ontologies (University, IT); ranking position of the true diagnosis did not significantly change the outcome.
agent_relevance: Humans are noisy oracles; an agent using a user as oracle needs checks for wrong answers. Fault ranking metrics alone mislead.

source: Rodler, Jannach, Schekotihin, Fleiss (2019) Are Query-Based Ontology Debuggers Really Helping Knowledge Engineers?
finding: 10 of the 14 participants who had the true diagnosis ranked high continued specifying test cases until one diagnosis was left, ignoring the instruction to mark it as soon as seen.
numbers: Study 1 group with true diagnosis visible: 10 of 14 kept going; did not identify it more often than the group where it was not visible.
limits: Small groups; no significant differences between the two ontologies.
agent_relevance: Seeing the right candidate is not the same as recognising it. Add explicit verification states.

source: Shchekotykhin, Fleiss, Rodler, Friedrich (2012) Direct computation of diagnoses for ontology debugging
finding: Direct diagnosis computation (Inv-QuickXplain, Inv-HS-Tree) skips conflict sets, which is needed when an ontology has many conflicts, such as in ontology alignment, where conflict set precomputation is infeasible.
numbers: Scalability test in Table 3, times in seconds, comparable to other systems; Inv-HS-Tree runs Inv-QuickXplain n times.
limits: Older (2012) and run only on ontology alignment cases.
agent_relevance: Alternative to conflict-then-hitting-set when conflicts are too many to list.

source: Rodler (2020) Understanding the QuickXPlain Algorithm: Simple Explanation and Formal Proof
finding: Explains the divide-and-conquer conflict finder (QuickXplain) that QXR uses with an LLM oracle. Downloaded, not read in detail.
numbers: Not recorded.
limits: Not read this session.
agent_relevance: QuickXplain is the subroutine cited for LLM conflict localization in QXR.

source: Garg et al. (2025) G-CSEA: Graph-Based Conflict Set Extraction for Pseudo-Boolean Models
finding: A conflict-driven method that traces constraint propagation to extract a compact conflict set, then optionally shrinks it with QuickXplain. Tested on workforce-scheduling infeasibility.
numbers: Conflict set 94.11% smaller than the original constraint set on average; with QuickXplain about 40% less IIS computation time than QuickXplain alone.
limits: Industrial scheduling, no LLM component, authors from a customer-service AI company.
agent_relevance: Shows pre-filtering with cheap conflict analysis before a costly oracle (an LLM call here) pays off.

source: Xu et al. (2026) Delta1 with LLM: symbolic and neural integration for credible and explainable reasoning
finding: Symbolic generator builds minimal unsatisfiable clause sets by construction in polynomial time; an LLM only verbalizes the contradiction and proof for people. Compared with MARCO and MUSer2 style MUS extractors that use hitting-set dualization.
numbers: Case studies in health care, compliance auditing, regulatory conformance, contract analysis (ten extra cases in appendix). No accuracy table found.
limits: Qualitative case studies only, not a measured benchmark.
agent_relevance: Pattern: symbolic core finds the minimal conflict, LLM explains it.

source: Pandey et al. (2026) Certified Multi-Source Integrity for Structured Agent Actions
finding: An LLM agent loop certifies structured actions using a minimum hitting set over evidence dependency sets, so copies of one source cannot fake agreement. Hitting set counts the fewest control domains an attacker must corrupt.
numbers: Five models in a real agent loop, 80 episodes each (54 with injection in one of N=5 sources, 26 clean). Injection followed: GPT-5.5 100%, Gemini 3.1 Pro 100%, Gemini 3.5 Flash 100%, Haiku 4.5 100%, Opus 4.8 0%. Naive unsafe: 72%, 100%, 98%, 100%, 0%. Certified unsafe: 0% for all.
limits: Security setting, not diagnosis proper; certifier false-abstain 0 to 12% under agreement rule, at most 4% under threshold rule.
agent_relevance: A hitting-set check is used inside an agent loop as a deterministic guard, not a model judgment.

source: Pandey et al. (2026) Certified Multi-Source Integrity (corroboration measurement)
finding: Apparent independent sources often collapse to few corruption-distinct domains once shared origin is counted.
numbers: Sanctions list: 70,966 entities, about three quarters rest on a single domain, about 15% show three or more; 450 npm packages: 16.4% appear to have three witnesses; PyPI 300 packages: 32.3%; none retain three once the shared GitHub root collapses, about 90% remain at exactly two.
limits: Upper-bound proxies; domain mapping is coarse.
agent_relevance: Count evidence by dependency, not by number of copies: a diagnosis idea (common-cause components) applied to sources.

source: Hipler, Leucker, Rodler (2026) A Unified Framework for Runtime Verification and Model-Based Diagnosis in Lola
finding: Encodes diagnosis problems as stream specifications so minimal diagnoses (minimal hitting sets of minimal conflicts) are computed at runtime from monitor output; covers multiple observations and temporal diagnosis.
numbers: No benchmark table read; framework paper.
limits: No LLM component; runtime-verification setting.
agent_relevance: Shows current hitting-set diagnosis work still has no LLM link; monitors plus diagnosis suggest a monitor-then-diagnose agent design.

source: arXiv title searches, Nov 2026 (author search 'Rodler diagnosis', 17 hits)
finding: Of 17 Rodler diagnosis papers listed (2010-2026), none mentions language models in the title. Only the 2026 QXR paper and a 2026 security paper use hitting sets with LLM oracles.
numbers: 17 listed items; arXiv searches for 'ontology debugging' (8 hits, latest 2019), 'QuickXplain' (4 hits), 'hitting set LLM agent' (2 hits) returned no LLM diagnosis-benchmark paper.
limits: Search limited: arXiv rate-limited after several queries; WebSearch budget exhausted. Absence of results is weak evidence.
agent_relevance: The LLM literature on efficient hitting-set diagnosis is thin; QXR is the main measured study found.
